name: Rescue
oneLine: Helping that keeps someone one-down: doing something you don't want to do, doing more than half the work, or helping before anyone's actually asked.
whatYouDid: You noticed that Meher's "you're the only one who could help me" had no actual request behind it, and chose a reply that asked what she'd already figured out for herself instead of just supplying the money.
confusion: People often hear "Rescue" and think it just means helping too much - but Steiner's test isn't the amount of help, it's whether the person was asked, whether both sides are doing their share, and whether the helper actually wants to. Refusing to help isn't automatically the fix either: a blunt no can tip straight into Persecution instead.

fromBook.quote: whether by going along with something she doesn't want to do, by doing more than 50% of the work, or by not asking for what is wanted

expand.definition: Steiner's three tests for Rescue: you're Rescuing when you do something you don't really want to do, when you do more than 50% of the work in helping someone, or when you help without being asked. Any one of the three is enough to make it a Rescue.
expand.otherFraming: Karpman's Drama Triangle names the same pattern from the other side: Rescuer and Victim are a matched pair, and the Rescuer role reliably curdles into Persecutor once resentment builds up - so refusing to Rescue is not the same move as switching to Persecute.
expand.tryThisToday: Next time you're about to help someone, pause and ask out loud what they want and what they're going to put toward it themselves, before you do anything.
